summary:
Clip mashups from iconic films demonstrate the 'hehe' laugh in different emotional contexts, each labelled (happy hehe, relaxed hehe, serious hehe). Humour comes from absurd juxtaposition and the running gag of the identical laugh across wildly different settings. Rapid cuts and on-screen text drive the joke.

Takeaways:
• Use the 'difference of' format with product variations or service tiers labelled with personality descriptors to make comparisons memorable
• Stack quick cuts from different contexts with minimal captions to create rhythm and pattern recognition
• Anchor original comedy to a recognisable trending sound or celebrity moment

use_case: Can be for Harbor Auto. What sound does an exhaust make, cut to a person saying the sound then cut to the car with the person's sound
summary:
A simple question-and-answer setup (3 seconds) cuts to a cinema-quality dinosaur close-up that matches the spoken sound effect, a comedic mismatch between casual banter and blockbuster spectacle.

Takeaways:
• Ask a relatable question, then cut to a wildly oversized visual match for the punchline
• Pair low-budget opening footage with a high-production cutaway to maximise surprise
• Make the spoken sound match exactly what appears on screen
• Works for product reveals: 'what does this car sound like?' then cut to the engine
• Keep the setup under 5 seconds

hook: I still can’t believe how low this plane was ✈️😳
use_case: I'd try this for Sunny Side Diner. the owner spots something 'flying dangerously low' outside, then catches a paper plane with a handwritten invitation to come in for breakfast. Keep the setup brief so the food or offer appears while the joke is still fresh.
summary:
Opens with genuine surprise and upward gazing, then subverts expectations by showing a paper plane instead of an aircraft. Setup takes two frames; silent with bold on-screen text.

Takeaways:
• Open with surprise directed off-screen to stop the scroll before viewers know it's a promotion
• Use misdirection so the reveal lands harder
• Keep the setup under five seconds
• Make the physical object the medium for your offer so the product becomes the joke

hook: Give me a color that starts with M
use_case: Can be for Harbor Auto and their blue cars
summary:
A call-and-response with a child who guesses 'blue' for a colour starting with M, triggering a reveal of stunning alpine lake footage. Wholesome, playful, visual payoff justifies the joke.

Takeaways:
• Open with an interactive-feeling question, then subvert with a visual payoff
• Genuine reactions from real people, especially kids, build relatability
• The colour game works for any brand with a distinctive colour identity, like the blue cars for Harbor Auto

hook: POV: Selling a new vehicle to Gen Z
summary:
POV sales video with a three-part reveal: energetic setup, then concrete features as text overlays (Apple CarPlay, backup camera, remote start) while the salesman nods along. Feels like insider knowledge rather than a pitch.

Takeaways:
• List concrete features as text overlays while talent nods on camera
• Open with high-energy body language and eye contact
• Frame it as 'what actually works' insider knowledge
• Show the dealership environment to establish credibility
• Structure reveals in threes

use_case: For Sunny Side Diner, a waiter appearing out of nowhere for any small inconvenience. For Harbor Auto, a salesperson appearing anytime someone glances at a car (maybe even from the road).
summary:
Uses the viral Spider-Man summon audio: cuts between everyday moments where the creator struggles, and her husband suddenly appears in the final frame. Builds anticipation through mundane scenes before the payoff.

Takeaways:
• Use trending audio with unexpected timing for surprise payoffs
• Cut between multiple locations to build familiarity
• Apply the 'sudden appearance' structure to service moments: waiter at table, salesperson at showroom
• Close with a reaction shot that completes the joke

A rating-system gimmick turns a dealership tour into an episodic ranking: each car gets a score out of 10 for an unexpected metric (soundproofing). Fast cuts and clean overlays keep momentum.

Takeaways:
• Use a rating or ranking system to structure a dealership tour
• Add clean numbered score overlays in a contrasting colour
• Feature multiple products in sequence for rapid discovery
• Lean into an unexpected testing angle to differentiate from typical reviews

hook: POV: The staff is too lazy to make content
use_case: Sunny Side Diner could have the owner ask the staff for one simple food video, then cut to a wildly dramatic stunt outside the restaurant before revealing the actual plate. The final beat can be the owner saying he only asked for a close-up of the pancakes.
summary:
Opens with a relatable workplace premise, undercuts it with an over-the-top stunt, then reveals the restaurant. Rapid pacing; the comedy is the contrast between lazy effort and ridiculous action.

Takeaways:
• Open with a relatable complaint, then subvert it with absurd visual excess
• Split the reveal across hook, action beat and brand reveal
• No voiceover needed; the visual mismatch carries the joke

use_case: I'd make a Sunny Side Diner breakfast-rush version. Follow a server moving between the counter, kitchen, and tables as plates come out. the owner can deliver the final plate with a mock race-finish reaction.
summary:
Hijacks motorsport broadcast language to frame rapid-fire taco prep as a race. Serious race footage sets the 'speed' frame, tight cuts of cooking feel impossibly fast by comparison, brand reveal at the end.

Takeaways:
• Borrow broadcast language from high-stakes contexts to frame mundane activities as dramatic
• Rapid montage and tight close-ups create perceived speed
• End with a clear brand and location reveal

hook: Caramel Macchiato, Strawberry Lemonade, Cinnamon Matcha
use_case: Sunny Side Diner could do the same with three colorful drinks or breakfast pairings, each labeled on screen as they land on the counter. the owner can take the final pick and ask the audience which one they would order first.
summary:
A pull-back reveal turns a menu into a visual lineup with clean labels and strong colour contrast. Team working in soft focus adds authenticity.

Takeaways:
• Reveal multiple products lined up so it feels like a curated choice
• Label each product with clean on-screen text
• Shoot from just below counter level with staff in soft focus
• End on 'which would you order first?' to drive comments

A bold, results-driven promise (2-week challenge) followed immediately by day one's exercise with clear on-screen instructions. Urgency, specificity and visual proof make the challenge feel achievable.

Takeaways:
• Lead with a concrete transformation promise (timeframe + result)
• Use numbered days to create a series viewers follow
• Layer instructional text directly on the demo so it works without sound

use_case: Could be a humorous employee video that shows their personalities and builds connection with the viewers.
summary:
Setup: an employee admits she's new. Payoff: she's been there for years. Casual behind-the-scenes clip with on-screen text and a reaction shot.

Takeaways:
• Use employee personality and self-deprecating humour to humanise the business
• Put the twist in the final frame
• Film behind the counter rather than staged
• Build a series with different team members using the same joke
